Twigs
twĭgz
n. pl. (the small shoots at the top of a tree)
From the Saxon twig, a small shoot, akin to twa, two, from the forking of a branch. Ezekiel uses the word twice, both times of the tender top of a cedar — once cropped off by an eagle in judgment, once cropped off by the LORD in promise.

Biblical Definition

Ezekiel's riddle of the two eagles turns on a handful of shoots. The first eagle is Babylon: “He cropped off the top of his young twigs, and carried it into a land of traffick; he set it in a city of merchants” (Ezekiel 17:4). The cropping is the deportation of Jehoiachin and the royal house to Babylon — a violent act performed by a foreign power for its own commercial ends. Then, at the end of the chapter, the identical gesture is made by another hand: “Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent” (Ezekiel 17:22). What Babylon did for plunder, God does for planting. The result is not a trading post but a kingdom: “In the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it: and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell” (Ezekiel 17:23). And the chapter closes by naming who is sovereign over every tree in the field: “And all the trees of the field shall know that I the LORD have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish: I the LORD have spoken and have done it” (Ezekiel 17:24).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines twig as a small shoot or branch of a tree or other plant, of no definite length or size.

expand to see more

TWIG, n. [Sax. twig.] A small shoot or branch of a tree or other plant, of no definite length or size.

BRANCH, n. A shoot, or arm of a tree; the offspring of a family; in Scripture, a title of the Messiah.

CROP, v.t. To cut off the ends of anything; to pull off; to pluck.

CEDAR, n. A large evergreen tree valuable for its durable and fragrant timber.

PLANT, v.t. To put into the ground and cover, as seed for growth; to set in the ground for growth; to settle; to establish.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 17:4 — "He cropped off the top of his young twigs, and carried it into a land of traffick; he set it in a city of merchants."

Ezekiel 17:22 — "Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent:"

Ezekiel 17:23 — "In the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it: and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell."

Ezekiel 17:24 — "And all the trees of the field shall know that I the LORD have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish: I the LORD have spoken and have done it."

Modern Corruption

The chapter is flattened into ancient political commentary, and the Messianic promise at its end is treated as a hopeful coda rather than the point the riddle was built to reach.

expand to see more

Ezekiel 17 is commonly handled as a coded editorial on sixth-century foreign policy: Zedekiah broke his oath to Nebuchadnezzar, sought Egyptian help, and was destroyed. All of that is in the chapter and is meant to be. But the historical-critical instinct to stop at the political layer removes the chapter's architecture. The riddle is constructed so that the same verb falls twice — an eagle crops a twig, and then the Lord GOD crops a twig — and the second cropping is the answer to the first. To read only the politics is to hear the question and walk out before the reply.

The tender twig planted on the high mountain of Israel, becoming a goodly cedar sheltering every wing, is Messianic, and the Reformed reading has always said so. What corrupts the passage is not usually a denial of that but a dilution of it: the promise is generalized into an assurance that history bends toward restoration. Ezekiel is more particular. A specific shoot is taken from a specific house by a specific hand and planted in a specific place, and the trees of the field learn from it who brings down and who exalts. The comfort of verse 24 is not that things improve; it is that the LORD has spoken and has done it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yeniqoth (H3127), young twigs or suckers; erez (H730), cedar; qataph (H6998), to crop off; tsammereth (H6788), the leafy top of a tree.

expand to see more

Hebrew yeniqoth (H3127) — young twigs, tender shoots; Ezekiel 17:4 and 17:22.

Hebrew tsammereth (H6788) — the foliage-top of a tree, the highest branch.

Hebrew qataph (H6998) — to crop off, pluck; the act of both eagle and LORD.

Hebrew shathal (H8362) — to transplant; I will plant it upon an high mountain.

Hebrew erez (H730) — cedar; the goodly cedar the twig becomes.

Usage

"“He cropped off the top of his young twigs” — Babylon takes the royal house."

"“I will crop off…a tender one” — the LORD repeats the gesture in promise."

"“I the LORD have spoken and have done it” — the seal on the riddle."
